newsitem.title: TOGO: Zaire talks due soon but no prior ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Zaire talks due soon but no prior ceasefire.

text.p: Zaire's rebels announced imminent talks with President Mobutu Sese Seko's shaky regime on Thursday but successfully resisted pressure to accept a prior ceasefire.
A two-day African summit on the Zaire crisis ended with a statement calling for immediate negotiations between the warring parties but did not insist on a ceasefire before the talks.

Five months into their revolt, Laurent Kabila's disciplined fighters control about a quarter of Zaire. Mobutu, 66 and weakened by prostate cancer, has watched his unpaid and demoralised army collapse in the field.

With copper-rich Shaba province now in their sights and Mobutu's departure after 32 years in office their priority, the rebels have no interest in agreeing to an early truce. They however accepted the principle of a ceasefire.

In a final declaration at the summit in Togo, African presidents "called for immediate negotiations between the government of Zaire and the Democratic Alliance for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL), leading to a ceasefire and complete cessation of hostilites".
South Africa or Togo were the likely venues for the talks.

Delegates from the warring factions met separately and then together on Thursday with the presidents of Nigeria, Togo and Cameroon with U.N. secretary-general Kofi Annan and his special representative, Mohamed Sahnoun.
"The two delegations have reiterated their commitment to accept the principle of a ceasefire and the principle of negotiations," a separate statement after those talks said.
Rebel officials in Kabila's eastern base at Goma said he left the border town by plane on Thursday evening with some of his closest advisers but they would not say where he had travelled to.
"It is only a short visit and he will soon return," one official told Reuters in Goma.

Kabila's senior representative at the summit, Bizima Karaha, said Mobutu remained a player. "There are some people who have a little power (left), in particular Mobutu and we would like to negotiate with him," he added.
"It's in his interests to negotiate his own departure," Gaetan Kakudji, the other Kabila representative in Lome, said.

There was no firm idea of the agenda of the imminent talks or indeed the participants. Mobutu is president but the opposition parties in Kinshasa also expect to be involved in negotiations with Kabila's rebel alliance.
Diplomats in Lome said the date for the start of negotiations and of a ceasefire would be announced after the two Zairean delegations had returned to base to consult.
In rebel-held Kisangani, the popular mood was for Kabila's men to press on with their advance.

Senior rebel sources there told Reuters there could be no ceasefire before negotiations in the form of a summit between Mobutu and Kabila, but they were willing to start talks between rival delegations to prepare the summit.
The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit gave the rebels their first major international platform.
Kabila scored more points in Paris when France, via its foreign ministry spokesman, changed its tone, dropping the term "rebels" and referring to them for the first time by their chosen name.
France has remained loyal to Mobutu throughout the rebellion but appears to have accepted there is now a high risk his 32-year reign is ending.
More than 1,000 Belgian, French and American troops are stationed in Congo, across the mighty Zaire river from Kinshasa, ready to evacuate their nationals if violence erupts.

Kinshasa is calm and the size and speed of the deployment have puzzled some observers. The troops' camp at Brazzaville's Maya-Maya camp is so congested that 200 of the 550 Belgian paratroopers have been moved to the oil town of Pointe Noire to make space, Belgian Colonel Wilfried Tersago told Reuters.
One of the five points in the U.N. peace plan for Zaire is for urgent action to help up to 370,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees of the Hutu tribe stranded in eastern Zaire.
The U.N. refugee agency reported alarming death rates among refugees at two sites and said the toll would only worsen unless rebels allow aid agencies to bring in more aid.

"The mortality rate at Tingi Tingi is 153 per 10,000 per day and at Amisi 48 per 10,000 per day. Refugees in a camp should be at between five and 10 deaths per 10,000 per day," UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg said in Kisangani.
"A mortality rate of 153 is very alarming. It is imperative the (rebel) alliance let us in to establish proper feeding to give these people care before they are repatriated," he said.
